sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: An upper trough crossing the Intermountain West early in the period is forecast to move steadily eastward, evolving into a deepening closed low and emerging into the central Plains through the second half of the period. Elsewhere, phased northern- and southern-stream troughing will continue to gradually vacate the East. At the surface, a deep/evolving low will pivot across the central Plains, crossing western Kansas through late afternoon and reaching the northeast Kansas/southeast Nebraska vicinity by the end of the period. Trailing from the low, a cold front will sweep across the southern Plains, while a warm front moves northeastward across the lower Missouri Valley and into the mid Mississippi and lower Ohio Valleys through 11/12Z.

sections.title: North-central Kansas northeast to western Iowa
sections.text: As the strengthening storm system shifts toward/into the Plains today, an intense deep-layer wind field will evolve across the risk area. However, rather scant low-level moisture will accompany the system, beneath stout capping. As such, convective development will remain suppressed across a large portion of the central and southern Plains despite an otherwise favorable synoptic setup. By mid afternoon, heating/mixing of the boundary layer combined with strong ascent focused near the surface low should permit localized weakening of the cap -- and eventual development of isolated convective cells. Initial development may occur over northwestern Kansas/southwestern Nebraska, but stronger/sustained updrafts appear more likely to initiate a bit later and a bit farther east, into the north-central Kansas/south-central Nebraska vicinity. Where updrafts can become sustained, the presence of very strong shear -- owing to veering/increasing flow with height to in excess of 70 kt from the southwest at mid levels during the afternoon -- will support strongly rotating updrafts. sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: The most important mid/upper-tropospheric feature for this forecast is a synoptic trough, now evident in moisture-channel imagery from portions of MT south-southwestward over western WY, UT, northwestern AZ, to northern Baja. An accompanying broad, messy 500-mb cyclone is apparent from the northern Rockies to UT, with several embedded vorticity maxima. This cyclone should distill to a more coherent low over eastern CO by 00Z, with trough southwestward over northern NM and southeastern AZ. By 12Z the mid/upper low should reach central/southwestern NE, with trough extending to near ELP. At the surface, the 11Z analysis showed an elongated area of low pressure over east-central CO and northwestern KS, along a wavy frontal zone. A warm front was drawn from there eastward across extreme northern KS, then east-southeastward to southern MO. The warm front should move northeastward to southeastern NE through this evening. The existing surface cyclone should move eastward during the day along the warm front, but become elongated and likely redevelop farther southwest on the boundary this afternoon over western KS. sections.title: Central Plains
sections.text: During mid/later afternoon, strengthening low-level convergence in the proximal northeastern sector of the surface cyclone, near the front, should lead to at least isolated to widely scattered thunderstorm development. Earliest convection may form over the northwestern KS/southwestern NE region; however the greatest potential for sustained and severe storms should be near the dryline/front intersection. A compact area of favorable buoyancy/shear overlap will exist in support of supercell potential, with very large, damaging hail being the main concern, and damaging gusts also possible. Forecast soundings suggest steep low/middle- level lapse rates and barely sufficient moisture for around 1000- 1500 J/kg MLCAPE to develop amidst strong lift at all scales. Effective-shear magnitudes around 70 kt are possible above the area of backed flow (along the front), with effective SRH locally exceeding 300 J/kg. A tornado cannot be ruled out, given the likelihood of at least one intense supercell and a vorticity/helicity-rich boundary layer probable near the warm front. sections.title: KS/NE
sections.text: An intense upper trough is digging across UT today, with a deep surface low expected to move from eastern CO into western KS. A substantial EML is spreading across the Plains today, capping the boundary-layer from convective development through the period in most areas. The one region where a few robust thunderstorms may form will be along and north of a strong surface boundary near the KS/NE border. Present indications are that elevated deep-convection will begin to form later this afternoon as lift increases behind a surging cold front over southwest NE and northwest KS. This activity will be in a region of impressive upper forcing, but weak thermodynamic support. Nevertheless, the strongest cells may produce hail. By 00z, there is a brief period when surface-based storms may develop in vicinity of the boundary in south-central NE and north-central KS. Most 12z CAM solutions show one or two storms forming in this area that quickly track northward atop the cold air mass and become elevated. sections.title: 20Z Update
sections.text: No changes have been made to the Enhanced and Slight risk areas across parts of northern KS into central/eastern NE. Latest short-term guidance continues to suggest that convection should form and quickly intensify across this region around 00Z (7 PM CDT). Large hail, some of which could be greater than 2 inches in diameter, appears to be the main threat. ..Gleason.. 04/10/2019 .PREV DISCUSSION... /ISSUED 1119 AM CDT Wed Apr 10 2019/

sections.title: Central Plains/Mid Missouri Valley
sections.text: An upper-level low over the central Rockies, evident on water vapor imagery, will continue to move eastward this evening as southwest mid-level flow remains over the southern and central Plains. A 75 to 100 kt mid-level jet in the base of the system will eject northeastward into the southern and central Plains this evening, helping to strengthen a 50 to 70 kt low-level jet. At the surface, a 984 mb low will move northeastward across Kansas. Surface dewpoints to the northeast of the low are in the lower to mid 50s F which is contributing to a small pocket of moderate instability where the RAP is estimating MLCAPE in the 1000 to 1500 J/kg range. Convection has initiated over the last hour along the northwestern edge of instability near a warm front. Strong low-level convergence along the front and large-scale ascent ahead of an approaching shortwave trough will continue to aide convective development early this evening. The HRRR is suggesting that a cluster of thunderstorms will organize and move northeastward into southeast Nebraska over the next 2 to 3 hours. mesoscale_discussions.summary: A few severe storms capable of mainly damaging hail may develop after 00Z.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: A surface low continues to deepen across central KS, and will track northeastward into southeast NE this evening. The synoptic setup overall is quite favorable for severe storms with steep lapse rates aloft, strong wind profiles, and lift. However, moisture is a major concern. GPS PW sensors indicate values approaching 0.60" near Wichita, but a band of relatively greater PW does exist near the stationary/developing warm front from near Kansas City into southeast NE. Recent visible imagery and radar shows skeletal convection forming near Russell KS as of 23Z, ahead of the low. The zone from here northeastward appears to have the greatest chance of severe storms capable of large hail. Supercells are possible, either elevated, or, surface based right along the front, with an enhanced risk of damaging hail. While low-level moisture is a concern, a conditional tornado risk still exists given favorable storm mode, steep lapse rates, lift along the boundary, and increasing low-level SRH.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: A hail threat will likely persist through the evening from northern Kansas into southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Significant large-scale lift persists across the region with a deep low moving into northeast KS. While boundary layer moisture has been marginal for severe weather, the presence of steep lapse rates and favorable lift has led to scattered severe storms producing hail up to Golf-Ball size. Extremely strong shear profiles exist across the warm sector and north of the stationary/warm front, but much of this SRH has been rendered in-effective. Continued warm advection around the cyclone will support elevated hail through the evening. The prospect for surface based storms appears low at this time. ..Jewell.. 04/11/2019 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...
